items.stem: Define the term "pyramid of biomass".
items.answer: A diagram showing the standing stock of dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time (e.g. g m⁻²)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a diagram showing the standing stock of dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time (e.g. g m⁻²). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: State two differences between a food chain and a food web.
items.answer: A food chain is a single linear sequence of feeding; a food web is many interconnected chains showing that organisms have several food sources and predators.
items.markingKey: A food chain is a single linear sequence of feeding; a food web is many interconnected chains showing that organisms have several food sources and predators. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why food webs are more realistic than food chains.
items.answer: Most organisms eat and are eaten by several species and may feed at more than one trophic level; webs show these interconnections and help predict knock-on effects. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most organisms eat and are eaten by several species and may feed at more than one trophic level; webs show these interconnections and help predict knock-on effects. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

(b) Energy declined at each level, giving an upright pyramid and showing large respiratory losses.

items.stem: Using Lake Victoria and the Nile perch as an example, explain the effect of adding a top predator to a food web.
items.answer: The introduction of Nile perch in the 1950s contributed to the extinction of about 200 species of endemic cichlid fish. A new predator restructured the food web, removing many herbivorous and detritivorous cichlids.
items.markingKey: Context (The introduction of Nile perch in the 1950s contributed to the extinction of about 200 species of endemic cichlid fish.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A new predator restructured the food web, removing many herbivorous and detritivorous cichlids. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the effect of adding a top predator to a food web.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Ecological pyramids are useful models of ecosystems."

items.stem: Producers in an East African savanna fix 60,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ as NPP. Assume an average transfer efficiency of 8% between all levels. (a) Calculate the energy available to tertiary consumers. (b) If a viable trophic level requires at least 10 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, determine how many levels of consumers the ecosystem could support. (c) Use the second law of thermodynamics to explain why food chains are rarely longer than four or five links.
items.answer: (a) 60,000 × 0.08³ = 30.7 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ (b) 3 consumer levels (c) at each transfer most energy is degraded to heat through respiration and cannot be reused; energy available falls geometrically until too little remains to sustain a population.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 repeated ×0.08, A1 30.7. (b) A1 3. (c) R1 second law / entropy, heat lost in respiration; R1 energy declines with each level so higher levels are limited.

items.stem: What are the main outputs of aerobic respiration?
options: Nitrogen and heat
Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide, water and energy (ATP and heat)
Oxygen and water
items.answer: Carbon dioxide, water and energy (ATP and heat)
items.markingKey: C. Respiration reverses photosynthesis.

items.stem: Explain why respiration is described as a transformation in terms of energy.
items.answer: Chemical energy in glucose is transformed into usable energy (ATP) for work and into heat, which is lost from the organism and eventually the ecosystem.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Chemical energy in glucose is transformed into usable energy (ATP) for work and into heat, which is lost from the organism and eventually the ecosystem. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline how the rate of photosynthesis is affected by light intensity, CO₂ and temperature.
items.answer: Each can be limiting: rate rises with light and CO₂ until another factor limits; enzymes work faster as temperature rises to an optimum, then denature.
items.markingKey: Each can be limiting: rate rises with light and CO₂ until another factor limits; enzymes work faster as temperature rises to an optimum, then denature. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Plants photosynthesise but do not respire." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Plants respire all the time, day and night; in light, photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration.
items.markingKey: Plants respire all the time, day and night; in light, photosynthesis usually exceeds respiration. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Experiment: an aquatic plant (Elodea) was placed at different distances from a lamp and bubbles of gas counted per minute: 10 cm 42; 20 cm 24; 30 cm 12; 40 cm 6; 50 cm 5.

Describe the relationship shown and explain it.
items.answer: Bubble rate falls as distance increases (light intensity falls with distance); light is the limiting factor for photosynthesis at greater distances.

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that increasing the efficiency of photosynthesis in crops is the best way to improve food security.
items.answer: Improved photosynthesis could help, but reducing waste and improving access are more immediate solutions.

Conclusion: Improved photosynthesis could help, but reducing waste and improving access are more immediate solutions. heterotroph

cellular respiration

items.stem: Distinguish between photosynthesis and chemosynthesis.
items.answer: Photosynthesis uses light energy to fix carbon; chemosynthesis uses energy from oxidising inorganic chemicals (e.g. H₂S at vents), so it can occur in darkness.

items.stem: Briefly describe hydrothermal vent communities on the East Pacific Rise and explain what it reveals about energy entering ecosystems without sunlight.
items.answer: Giant tube worms (Riftia) host chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidise hydrogen sulfide to fix carbon in total darkness. Chemosynthesis replaces photosynthesis as the energy source, supporting dense communities 2,500 m deep.
items.markingKey: Context (Giant tube worms (Riftia) host chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidise hydrogen sulfide to fix carbon in total darkness.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Explain how photosynthesis and respiration link the carbon cycle and energy flow in an ecosystem. [7]
items.answer: Photosynthesis transforms light to chemical energy and fixes carbon; respiration releases energy as heat and CO₂; carbon is recycled while energy flows; NPP = GPP − R; seasonal CO₂ cycle.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Photosynthesis transforms light to chemical energy and fixes carbon; respiration releases energy as heat and CO₂; carbon is recycled while energy flows; NPP = GPP − R; seasonal CO₂ cycle. gross secondary productivity (GSP)

decomposer
items.answer: net primary productivity (NPP)

items.stem: "An old-growth forest has the highest net productivity because it has the most biomass." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Mature forests have high biomass but high respiration, so net productivity is lower than in younger, rapidly growing stages.
items.markingKey: Mature forests have high biomass but high respiration, so net productivity is lower than in younger, rapidly growing stages. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between net primary productivity and gross primary productivity.
items.answer: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; NPP is what remains after plant respiration (NPP = GPP − R) and is the energy available to consumers.
items.markingKey: GPP is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis; NPP is what remains after plant respiration (NPP = GPP − R) and is the energy available to consumers. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using the Amazon rainforest vs the Sahara Desert as an example, explain climatic control of primary productivity.
items.answer: Tropical rainforest NPP is about 2,200 g m⁻² yr⁻¹ compared with less than 90 g m⁻² yr⁻¹ in hot deserts. Productivity is limited by water in deserts but not in rainforests where warmth, light and rainfall are all high.
items.markingKey: Context (Tropical rainforest NPP is about 2,200 g m⁻² yr⁻¹ compared with less than 90 g m⁻² yr⁻¹ in hot deserts.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Productivity is limited by water in deserts but not in rainforests where warmth, light and rainfall are all high. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to climatic control of primary productivity.

items.stem: Energy budget for a dairy cow grazing a pasture: grass eaten 480 kJ per day; energy lost in faeces 230 kJ per day; energy used in respiration 140 kJ per day. (a) Calculate gross secondary productivity (GSP). (b) Calculate net secondary productivity (NSP). (c) Calculate the percentage of the food eaten that becomes new biomass and suggest why it is low.
items.answer: (a) GSP = food eaten − faecal loss = 480 − 230 = 250 kJ per day (b) NSP = GSP − R = 250 − 140 = 110 kJ per day (c) 22.9%; most assimilated energy is respired (movement, homeostasis, in endotherms keeping warm) and lost as heat.
items.markingKey: (a) M1 GSP = food eaten − faecal loss, A1 250. (b) A1 110. (c) A1 22.9%; R1 respiration/heat loss (higher in endotherms).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "bioaccumulation"?
options: A diagram showing the standing stock of dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time (e.g. g m⁻²)
The gain by consumers in energy or biomass per unit area per unit time remaining after allowing for respiratory losses: NSP = GSP − R
A diagram showing the flow of energy through each trophic level per unit area per unit time (e.g. kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹); it is never inverted

items.stem: Outline why biomagnification affects top predators most.
items.answer: Each consumer eats many prey, and the persistent pollutant is stored rather than excreted, so the dose increases at each trophic level; top predators also live long and accumulate over their lifetime.
items.markingKey: Each consumer eats many prey, and the persistent pollutant is stored rather than excreted, so the dose increases at each trophic level; top predators also live long and accumulate over their lifetime. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.answer: Humans eating top-level fish received high doses of mercury that had concentrated along the food chain.

items.stem: With reference to DDT in Long Island Sound, USA (Woodwell, 1967), explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in biomagnification. [7]

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (the Peruvian upwelling): Cold, nutrient-rich water rising off Peru supports some of the world's highest marine productivity and the anchoveta fishery (up to about 10 million t a year).

Explain what this information reveals about nutrient limitation of marine productivity.
items.answer: Upwelling brings nitrates and phosphates to the sunlit surface, removing the nutrient limitation found in most of the open ocean.
items.markingKey: Upwelling brings nitrates and phosphates to the sunlit surface, removing the nutrient limitation found in most of the open ocean. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to nutrient limitation of marine productivity, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: Concentrations of methylmercury measured along a food chain: seawater: 0.0001 ppm; phytoplankton: 0.004 ppm; zooplankton: 0.032 ppm; herring: 0.16 ppm; harbour seals: 1.92 ppm. (a) Calculate how many times more concentrated methylmercury is in harbour seals than in herring. (b) Outline why the concentration increases along the chain.
items.answer: (a) 1.92 / 0.16 = 12 times (b) methylmercury is persistent and fat-soluble, so it is stored in fatty tissue (bioaccumulation) and not excreted; each predator eats many prey, so the amount accumulates at each trophic level (biomagnification).
items.markingKey: (a) A1 ×12. (b) R1 persistent/fat-soluble, not broken down or excreted; R1 consumers eat large quantities of prey so concentration increases.

items.stem: With reference to sea otters and kelp forests in the Aleutian Islands, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in top-down control in food webs (trophic cascade). [7]
items.answer: When orcas began eating otters in the 1990s, otter numbers fell by about 90%, urchins increased and kelp density declined sharply. Removing the top predator released the herbivores from predation, which overgrazed the producers. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: When orcas began eating otters in the 1990s, otter numbers fell by about 90%, urchins increased and kelp density declined sharply. Removing the top predator released the herbivores from predation, which overgrazed the producers. items.stem: Outline the inputs, outputs and transformations of photosynthesis as a system.
items.answer: Inputs: light energy, CO₂, water; transformation: light to chemical energy, inorganic to organic carbon; outputs: glucose (stored chemical energy), O₂, heat.
items.markingKey: Inputs: light energy, CO₂, water; transformation: light to chemical energy, inorganic to organic carbon; outputs: glucose (stored chemical energy), O₂, heat.

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Concentrations of PCBs (mg/kg lipid) in an Arctic food chain: seawater < 0.000001; zooplankton 0.04; Arctic cod 0.3; ringed seal 1.5; polar bear 20.

Calculate the magnification factor between ringed seals and polar bears.
items.markingKey: 20 / 1.5 ≈ 13 times. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Give one strength and one limitation of the claim that food webs are more resilient when they contain many top predators.
items.answer: Healthy predator populations generally increase resilience, but diversity at all trophic levels matters.
items.markingKey: For: predators regulate herbivores and prevent overgrazing. Against: too many predators can deplete prey. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that photosynthesis is the most important process in the biosphere. [9]
items.answer: Photosynthesis is fundamental, but ecosystems depend on its balance with respiration and decomposition.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: captures almost all energy entering ecosystems; produces oxygen and removes CO₂; supports food production. Arguments challenging it: respiration and decomposition are equally essential for cycling; chemosynthesis supports some ecosystems. A supported conclusion might be: Photosynthesis is fundamental, but ecosystems depend on its balance with respiration and decomposition. items.stem: Why can a pyramid of numbers be inverted?
options: Producers are always small
Biomass is created by consumers
One large producer (e.g. an oak tree) can support many small herbivores
Energy increases at higher levels
items.answer: One large producer (e.g. an oak tree) can support many small herbivores
items.markingKey: C. Numbers ignore organism size.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "photosynthesis"?
options: The total gain in energy or biomass per unit area per unit time fixed by photosynthesis in green plants
The gain by consumers in energy or biomass per unit area per unit time remaining after allowing for respiratory losses: NSP = GSP − R
The process by which producers use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
A diagram showing the standing stock of dry mass of organisms at each trophic level at one time (e.g. g m⁻²)
items.answer: The process by which producers use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
items.markingKey: C. "photosynthesis" is the process by which producers use light energy to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.

items.stem: Which ecosystem has the highest NPP per unit area?
options: Tropical rainforest (or estuaries and swamps)
Tundra
Desert
Open ocean
items.answer: Tropical rainforest (or estuaries and swamps)
items.markingKey: A. Rainforest NPP is about 2,200 g m⁻² yr⁻¹; open ocean about 125.

items.stem: Briefly explain why biomagnification affects top predators most.
items.answer: Each consumer eats many prey, and the persistent pollutant is stored rather than excreted, so the dose increases at each trophic level; top predators also live long and accumulate over their lifetime.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each consumer eats many prey, and the persistent pollutant is stored rather than excreted, so the dose increases at each trophic level; top predators also live long and accumulate over their lifetime. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline why top carnivores are often rare and vulnerable.
items.answer: Only a small fraction of energy reaches the top of food chains, so populations are small; they need large ranges, reproduce slowly, accumulate toxins (biomagnification) and are often persecuted.
items.markingKey: Only a small fraction of energy reaches the top of food chains, so populations are small; they need large ranges, reproduce slowly, accumulate toxins (biomagnification) and are often persecuted. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Respiration creates energy." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Energy cannot be created (first law); respiration transforms chemical energy into ATP and heat.
items.markingKey: Energy cannot be created (first law); respiration transforms chemical energy into ATP and heat. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why tropical rainforests have high NPP while deserts have low NPP.
items.answer: Rainforests have high, constant temperatures, high rainfall and high light all year, so photosynthesis is fast and continuous; deserts are limited by water (and sometimes extreme temperature), so plant cover and photosynthesis are low.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rainforests have high, constant temperatures, high rainfall and high light all year, so photosynthesis is fast and continuous; deserts are limited by water (and sometimes extreme temperature), so plant cover and photosynthesis are low. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between biomagnification and bioaccumulation.
items.answer: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a pollutant within one organism over its lifetime; biomagnification is the increase in concentration from one trophic level to the next.
items.markingKey: Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a pollutant within one organism over its lifetime; biomagnification is the increase in concentration from one trophic level to the next. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Case study extract - the Mauna Loa CO₂ record: Atmospheric CO₂ shows a seasonal cycle of about 6 ppm, falling in the northern summer and rising in winter.

Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain how this case illustrates the global balance of photosynthesis and respiration.
items.answer: In the northern summer photosynthesis by the large land area of northern forests exceeds respiration, drawing down CO₂; in winter respiration dominates.
items.markingKey: In the northern summer photosynthesis by the large land area of northern forests exceeds respiration, drawing down CO₂; in winter respiration dominates. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to the global balance of photosynthesis and respiration, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Mean NPP (g m⁻² yr⁻¹) and area (million km²): tropical rainforest 2,200 and 17.0; temperate forest 1,250 and 12.0; savanna 900 and 15.0; tundra 140 and 8.0; open ocean 125 and 332.0.

Calculate the total annual NPP of the open ocean and of tropical rainforest (in 10¹⁵ g, i.e. Pg).
items.markingKey: Ocean: 125 × 332 × 10¹² m² = 41.5 × 10¹⁵ g ≈ 41.5 Pg; rainforest: 2,200 × 17 × 10¹² = 37.4 Pg. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: In a kelp forest, sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat kelp. Predict and explain the effect of removing sea otters.
items.answer: Urchin numbers rise without predation, they overgraze kelp, forming "urchin barrens"; fish and invertebrates that depend on kelp decline - a trophic cascade.
items.markingKey: Urchin numbers rise without predation, they overgraze kelp, forming "urchin barrens"; fish and invertebrates that depend on kelp decline - a trophic cascade.

items.stem: Describe how the GPP of an aquatic plant could be estimated using light and dark bottles.
items.answer: Measure initial dissolved O₂; incubate one clear bottle (photosynthesis + respiration → net production) and one dark bottle (respiration only); GPP = (light − initial) + (initial − dark) = light − dark.
items.markingKey: Measure initial dissolved O₂; incubate one clear bottle (photosynthesis + respiration → net production) and one dark bottle (respiration only); GPP = (light − initial) + (initial − dark) = light − dark.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that NPP is the most useful measure of the value of an ecosystem. [9]
items.answer: NPP is a valuable ecological measure but must be combined with biodiversity, stock and ecosystem-service measures.

items.stem: "International bans are the most effective way to prevent harm from persistent pollutants." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: Bans are essential, but must be combined with clean-up, monitoring and testing of new chemicals before release.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: Stockholm Convention covers 30+ chemicals; peregrines recovered after DDT bans. Arguments challenging it: legacy pollutants persist for decades; new chemicals (PFAS) emerge faster than bans; trade-offs (DDT for malaria).
